text.tspan: spring → crown wheel → verge → the tail wags in place · purple = mechanism
SIDE VIEW – cut away · from the fish’s right · scale 1.4 : 1
tail section swings on the verge pin
THE TRICK – A VERGE ESCAPEMENT (as in the first clocks)
but only one tooth per wag
b TOOTH PUSHES THE UPPER PALLET
from above · solid: upper pallet, top teeth (→) · dashed: lower, bottom teeth (←)
① Winding the nose key coils the spring; the click stops it running back.
② The spring turns the barrel, but its 21 crown teeth have to get past the two pallets.
③ A top tooth shoves the upper pallet → the tail swings; that swings the lower pallet
into a bottom tooth → it shoves back → the tail swings back (b ↔ c).
④ One tooth per wag: the spring can only let go a little at a time, so it keeps going.
① Push the fish onto its anemone
② Fin UP (locked). Turn the nose
③ Push the pectoral fin DOWN →
④ Fin back UP stops it any time.
Too fast? A heavier tail wags slower
100 % printed; every part fits the egg
Built: 110 long, 79 tall → bigger than the egg
Trigger = fin lever, no removable pin
Opening the head lets the spring go
Snap fits: no glue, no tools
Clownfish don’t cruise: they hover beside their anemone,
sculling with quick tail beats. This one does the same on its
anemone stand, and its white bands hide the moving joint.
ENGG*2100 F26 · Design & Build · Concept Sketch
Biomimicry – clownfish hovering at its anemone
Spring toy, swims in place ≥ 5 s
